# 09-karsa — sources

Back-test entry `09-karsa.yaml`: Karsa, buying and saving dollar stablecoins where the local currency inflates
(YC Winter 2025). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only. Quotes are verbatim from the page named; "Author's
choice" marks the smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent.

Main sources:
- [HN] Launch HN: Karsa (YC W25), 2025-01-30, 215 comments — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42879661 (a comment is cited by its own item URL)
- [LYC] Launch YC: Karsa, the global dollar account — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/MgV-karsa-the-global-dollar-account
- [YCP] YC company page — https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/karsa (now "a stablecoin neobank")
- [DAWN23] Dawn, on digital currencies in Pakistan as "a high-tech replacement for hawala-hundi" (headline shortened here), 2023-10-30 — https://www.dawn.com/news/1784968
- [AAJ] Aaj News, "Dollars disappear from open market due to hoarding", 2022-12-15 — https://english.aaj.tv/news/30306930
- [DAWN21] Dawn, "Biometric proof must for buying $500 or above: SBP", 2021-10 — https://www.dawn.com/news/1650577/biometric-proof-must-for-buying-500-or-above-sbp
- [NAYA] NayaPay help, the SBP's annual card limit — https://help.nayapay.com/article/242-what-is-the-annual-card-based-international-transactions-limit-set-by-the-sbp
- [ARAB] Arab News, "Pakistan says has no plans to freeze foreign currency accounts", 2023-06-12 — https://www.arabnews.pk/pakistan/pakistan-says-has-no-plans-to-freeze-foreign-currency-accounts-2320266

## Market

The public material supports **Pakistan** best: the founder's family ([HN] "his uncle in Pakistan"; [LYC] "Shahryar's
family in Pakistan still acutely faces this problem"), the first live sellers ([YCP] "Pakistan, India, Nigeria,
Kenya, Paraguay"), the PKR page discussed in the thread, and the most press on the problem. The segment and all twenty
respondents are in Pakistan. The eval's loader (`instructions/corpus.py`, `MARKET_CURRENCY`) knows only GB, US, IE, FR,
DE, IN, CA and AU, so per the brief the `market` line is **US** (`language: en-US`) and every money value is in USD.
Dollars are also the unit these savers think and buy in (the fee is 1% of the dollars bought). keel-cloud's own
`Market` table does not know PK either, though `Market.chosen` would take PK with an explicit currency.

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** People in Pakistan who earn in rupees and save.
   [HN] "when Shahryar tried explaining [it] to his uncle in Pakistan, it was all jargon until he explained
   stablecoins, which immediately clicked." → `roles[saver]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`.

2. **What (the job).** Keep savings from losing value.
   [HN] "buy and save in stablecoins to protect against currency instability and inflation"; "Over a billion people
   live in countries with severe inflation and are unable to protect their wealth due to strict capital controls."
   → `context.job`, `statements.problem`.

3. **When / where.** When they have rupees left over and want dollars, with the bank and the exchange companies in the
   way. [HN] "earning in a currency thatʼs inflating 20-30% year-over-year"; "good luck getting a foreign currency
   account." [AAJ] dollars "not being readily available in the open market". [DAWN21] exchange companies must "conduct
   biometric verification for all foreign currency sale transactions equivalent to $500 and above". [NAYA] card-based
   international transactions "of up to USD 30,000 per year", "per individual, not per card".
   → `context.circumstance`. Author's choice: the occasion "payday", the window {3, MONTHS}, Frequency 2 to 3 months out
   of 3, and Prevalence `p_60_80` ("Most"): no public figure says how often.

4. **Which people (the comparable group).** [HN] "(1) earning in a currency thatʼs inflating 20-30% year-over-year, (2)
   whoʼs structurally limited from dollar access, and (3) makes payments abroad regularly". → `context.segment`
   (narrowed to Pakistan, the market chosen; condition 3 becomes the Importance rival "Paying for things abroad").

5. **Who pays.** The saver, alone. [HN] "We currently take a 1% transaction fee". → `persona.decision_maker:
   same_person`, Buyer and payer "Nobody else". Author's choice: no other role is named.

6. **Mechanism.** [HN] "Karsa looks and feels like a bank/currency exchange to an average user—they choose an amount
   and buy dollar-denominated stablecoins at a market price. But under the hood, we route our supply from a network of
   verified peer-to-peer stablecoin traders"; "A seller sets their price and deposits money in an escrow smart
   contract"; the buyer "has to send a fiat payment (e.g., bank transfer, payment app, etc.) to the sellerʼs local
   account + upload a photo for verification"; "we ... release the escrowed stablecoins to a digital wallet weʼve
   created for the buyer." → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`, the Compatibility and Adoption friction items
   (the ID card and payment photo item comes from the same step and from [HN] "we do KYC"). Commitment's step "buy a
   small first amount of dollars" is the author's.

7. **Price.** [HN] "We currently take a 1% transaction fee, though we eventually intend to adjust it proportionally to
   regional FX rates." → `commercial.price` {1, 3, month}: author's arithmetic, 1% of about $100 to $300 of dollars
   bought a month (the amount is the author's choice). Existing sacrifice {5, 15, month}: the premium paid today,
   from [DAWN23] (the PKR-to-USDT premium over the official rate reportedly widened from Rs5-6 to Rs8-9) and [HN] (India:
   "the bid-ask spreads are calamitous - to the tune of 5-6% per side" — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42885086),
   taken as 3% to 5% of the same $100 to $300 (author's arithmetic). Ability to pay is derived by code (7% to 60%).

8. **Occasions.** [HN] "Users in these countries already use exchanges like Binance almost like a dollar checking
   account" — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42880301 ; a user in Bolivia: "there’s a limit of 50 USD on USD
   transactions per week for each bank" — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42881375 (outside the chosen market, so
   it shaped the statement, not a respondent); [DAWN23] "A need for wealth preservation in the face of high inflation and
   currency devaluation"; "a high share of activity happening in Pakistan is through peer-to-peer exchanges".

- Nadia Rizvi → a sceptic whose way works: "if you live in a jurisdiction where it’s easy and safe to get and hold substantial amounts of USD, this is not for you" — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42884769 ; the easy bank-app conversion described in https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42885756 . Her old Dubai account is the author's detail.

- Danish Rajput → the 5-6% spread comment — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42885086 (India, transposed); the bank's call is the author's detail, after [HN] "Bank transfers do get lost and require chasing banks" — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42880264
- Rubina Gill → [HN] post, "earning in a currency thatʼs inflating 20-30% year-over-year" and "good luck getting a foreign currency account"; her pay and amount are the author's.
- Zainab Changezi → author's invention, filling a gap: a household decision (Buyer and payer "had to agree") and a dealer found through family, after the grey-market dealers of https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42884769
- Asad Khattak → "this business idea isn’t to just leave a buyer holding the bag" — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42883197 ; the partial release is the author's detail.
- Ghulam Sarwar Bhatti → [HN] the founder's relative in Pakistan for whom stablecoins "immediately clicked" once explained; a relative abroad does it for him (the Current-solution escape). His name and details are the author's.
- Sadia Awan → author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped (rather_not_say) story; money is private.
- Waqas Mirza → author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, habitual story with no one occasion (GUESSED).
- Nasreen Bibi → gate No: nothing left over to save, after "They need food and water" — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42884419
- Tariq Lodhi → gate No: saves in gold, not dollars, after "why not gold?" — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42882904 ; author's invention beyond that.
- Saima Butt → author's invention, filling a gap: gate No, saves through a rotating savings committee in rupees.
- Junaid Malik → gate No: already paid in dollars and keeps them there, after [DAWN23] on freelancers paid in USDT.
- Areeba Soomro → author's invention, filling a gap: gate No, a student with no savings in the window.

No respondent carries the name of a commenter, customer or founder.

## Open
- Market: the loader knows no PK currency, so the entry is US / en-US with dollars while the segment and every
  respondent are in Pakistan. A Keel study in Pakistan would ask in English or Urdu and might price in rupees; that is
  not tested here.
- The verdict was scripted to be plausible and not obviously "build": the problem holds (most had it, most say getting
  savings into dollars is one of their two, today's ways fall short); the solution splits on paying a seller they have
  never met (eight of thirteen would); the commercial side splits on what the problem costs them today (several pay
  little or nothing besides inflation) and on taking a first step, while the 1% fee itself holds. This is the author's
  reading of the thread's sceptics, not a measured result.
- Two respondents transpose accounts from India (the KYC wall, the spread) to Pakistan; the Bolivian $50-a-week limit
  shaped the founder's statement only.
- Existing sacrifice picks use `period: quarter` (the corpus's convention), although the registry's recall period for a
  monthly cost reads "last month"; the values are three months' worth.
- DAWN23's headline is shortened in the source list: its first word holds a string banned from these files.
- The amount bought a month ($100 to $300), the occasion "payday", the window and the Prevalence bin are the author's.

insights.line: What made the others more pressing?

whys.g1: Both answers name bills that keep coming each month while pay stays flat, so putting them together under the plain name "Monthly bills keep coming" is how I would sort them, even though Farhan also stresses keeping what's left safe after being cheated by a seller.
whys.g2: There is no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line, so nothing was grouped that should not have been.

founder.order_why: The flow runs sensibly from context to problem to sending, but the window question (screen 4) sits between two context screens with the same heading, which splits the context step in an odd way.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 5 both show 'Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies.'
founder.missing: Where-you-sell (screen 2) never let me pick Pakistan or rupees, so the study says US while every saver is in Pakistan, and nothing asked which language (English or Urdu) savers should be asked in.

PRIMARY.order_why: Screen 5 says 'think of the time you described' but I was never asked to describe a specific time, and asking what I'd most like made easier (screen 4) before asking how the conversion went (screen 5) puts the wish ahead of the story; screens 1 and 2 are also both labelled '1 of 4', and the last screen assumes it 'works for me' when I had said it was hard.
PRIMARY.asked_twice: Screens 2 and 5 both ask how turning leftover rupees into dollars went, once as yes/no and once open-ended; screen 3 repeats screen 2's question as a count.
PRIMARY.missing: How I actually buy dollars (Binance P2P, open-market dealer, a relative abroad), how much over the official rate I pay, how much effort each trade takes (the chats to confirm details with every buyer or seller), whether dollars were even available when I wanted them, and where I keep the dollars once I have them with no foreign currency account.

screens.why1: Naming the project is the natural first step before anything else is asked.
screens.why2: "What should we call this project?" is plain to any founder on first reading.
screens.why3: I know my own company's name and what it does, so I can answer it at once.
screens.why4: A free-text box with no options, chips or rows to judge.
screens.why5: My typed name, Karsa with its tagline about saving in dollars when your currency keeps falling, is kept as I wrote it.

screens.why1: Right after naming the project, asking where I'll sell first is the obvious next question, since it sets the currency and language of everything after.
screens.why2: "Where will you sell this first?" is plain to any founder; I'd answer Pakistan at once.
screens.why3: I know exactly where my first customers are: my uncle's Pakistan, earning in rupees.
screens.why4: The country list has no Pakistan, so my true answer is missing and I'm pushed onto US, a market where nobody has my customers' problem.
screens.why5: The kicker keeps my words, but the recorded market reads US when my savers and their rupees are in Pakistan, so the dollars-and-English framing drifts from what I'd have typed.
screens.instead: Where will you sell this first? [country picker that includes Pakistan, with currency PKR or USD and language English or Urdu]

screens.why1: Before anything is tested I would expect Keel to pin down who, what and when, so asking for the context as the first real step is obviously right.
screens.why2: Four short phrases about my own customers, in words I use myself (saver, rupees, foreign currency account); only "boundary" is slightly abstract but it reads fine first time.
screens.why3: It asks about my own idea and my own customers, Pakistanis earning in rupees who want dollars, which I know better than anything.
screens.why4: The screen shows four boxes to type in and a read-back, with no options, chips or value box to judge.
screens.why5: The read-back keeps my segment, job, circumstance and the 3-month window and quietly fixes my typos ("lossing", "accountt") without changing a word's meaning; only the clumsy "that have... who earn" ordering reads a little stiff.

screens.why1: Right after defining who and when, it makes sense to fix how far back a saver's last payday-with-rupees-left-over should count, and nothing earlier asked this.
screens.why2: "Episode" is a researcher's word, not mine; I would say "the last time they had rupees left over", though the intro makes it clear enough on a second read.
screens.why3: I know my savers convert when money is left over after pay, roughly monthly, so I can set a window from what I know of how often that happens.
screens.why4: A count and a unit cover every sensible window, and 3 months fits a monthly payday habit without making people strain to remember.
screens.why5: The summary keeps my segment, job, circumstance and 3-month window; only the word order and "that have" read a little clumsy, and the meaning is unchanged.
screens.instead: How far back should people look for the last time they had rupees left over and wanted dollars? [count] [days / weeks / months]

screens.why1: After I typed the context and picked the window, a read-back for me to confirm before anything is tested is exactly where it belongs.
screens.why2: Rupees, dollars, foreign currency account and savings losing value are my own words; the only snag is the clumsy 'that have... who earn' order, which I still read at once.
screens.why3: It is my own study and my uncle's situation, so I can judge it immediately.
screens.why4: 'Yes, that's it' with a way to edit is all a confirmation card needs, and it fits.
screens.why5: The read-back keeps all four fields and the 3-month window, and it correctly says Pakistan rather than the US market line; tying the job to the moment they turn rupees into dollars is a slight tightening of my words, not a change in meaning.

screens.why1: Step 2 opens on the problem, and this is my own problem statement played back right after I set the context, so it is obvious why it is here.
screens.why2: Every word is one I use myself (rupees, foreign currency account, exchange companies, Binance, premium), and it reads clean once my typos are fixed, though it is one long sentence.

screens.why3: This is the problem I pitched from my uncle's and my family's lives in Pakistan, so I can judge every clause of it on sight.

screens.why1: After asking how many savers hit the problem, it makes sense to ask how often each one hits it, and a monthly count fits a payday rhythm.
screens.why2: The words are mine (saver, rupees, dollars), but 'in how many months did a typical saver have rupees left over and could not easily turn them into dollars' packs two conditions into one long clause and needs a second read.

screens.why2: The choices are clear to me, but each label runs into its description with no break ('People I know by name I send each one their own link'), and 'the Contacts page' is a Keel word I have not seen in this flow, so I read it twice.
screens.why3: I know exactly who I would reach (my family's circle in Pakistan, people I can name one by one, or a WhatsApp group where savers already talk), so I can answer from my own situation.
screens.why4: Named people, a Keel-found list, and one open link posted to a group are distinct and cover how I would actually reach Pakistani savers, with the group option fitting WhatsApp or Facebook groups.
screens.why5: Nothing here changes my saver, my job or my segment, and it leaks nothing of the product to a respondent.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? — People I know by name: I send each one their own link · People from a Keel search: pick a list, Keel makes a link for each, you send them · A group (WhatsApp, Facebook): one open link posted where they already are; each signs in with Google

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'People disagree' is stated with 'median 2 months out of 3' beside it, but that median sits inside my own '2 to 3 months', so the number shown does not explain the verdict; the deciding fact (4 of 7 against a bar of 5, one short) is only down on the Frequency card.
screens.why_b2: The tally '3 holding · 1 split · 7 people answered' is plain, and each card shows its count against the bar, but the Frequency card's line stacks median, below, at-or-beyond, bar and 'short' and needs a second read to see what is counted.
screens.why_b3: Prevalence, Frequency, Importance and Current solution carry the beliefs I checked in my own words: leftover rupees into dollars, inflation as one of their two, today's way falling short.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what a split on how often it bites means for Karsa (for example, whether people buy dollars only on some paydays and what that does to a per-transaction fee); 'What it measures' only explains how the verdict is computed.
screens.why_b5: The 7 stays visible, but nobody says 7 is a small number, and the two cards that only just reach the bar at 5 of 7 get the same 'Holding up' as the 7 of 7 on Prevalence.
screens.instead: Lead with 'Frequency is one short: 4 of 7 hit it on 2 or more months of 3, bar 5', mark Importance and Current solution as just at the bar, note only 7 people answered, and say what to check next, such as whether savers buy dollars every payday or only some.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up above your band' sits right beside '7 of 7 said yes · bar 5 of 7', and the count line's 'a lean, not a call' matches it.
screens.why_b2: Seven cells all marked for me, the marker at 5 and the 0-to-7 axis show what is counted (said yes), over how many (7) and where my bar sits at first look.
screens.why_b3: I recognise the occasion, turning leftover rupees into dollars, but I never checked a 'Prevalence' belief, and '6 to 7 in 10' is narrower than the 'most' I meant.
screens.why_b4: The So line only points me to the next two cards; it never says that the problem being common among my savers means I can stop proving it exists.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is shown throughout, the small group is called 'a lean, not a call', and 7 of 7 is not stretched beyond these seven people.
screens.instead: All 7 of 7 found it hard to get dollars in the last 3 months, which is above your 5-of-7 bar but only a lean with 7 people; stop proving it is common and check how often it happens and whether it is in their top two.

screens.why_b1: The status 'People disagree' sits right beside the deciding count: 4 of 7 at or beyond what I said, against a bar of 5 of 7, so 1 short.
screens.why_b2: The axis of months out of 3 and the 7 cells are plain, but the median label sits between 2 and 3, the legend reads as a jumble ('what you said at what you said short of it'), and the bar's '(at least 2 in 3)' is easy to confuse with '2 months out of 3' until I read it again.
screens.why_b3: The line uses my own circumstance words ('turn leftover rupees into dollars') and my 2-to-3-months band, but Frequency is not among the beliefs listed as checked on the way in, and the question's tag 'the most recent time it happened' does not match a count of months.
screens.why_b4: 'Whether it matters is the next card' sends me elsewhere instead of telling me what 4 of 7 means for selling to someone who saves every payday versus only now and then.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible, the screen says 'a small group: a lean, not a call', and it calls the result a split rather than a hold.
screens.instead: 4 of 7 struggle to get dollars in 2 or 3 of the last 3 months, 1 short of your bar; with 7 people that's a lean, so ask the 3 who struggled less whether they simply had less left over to save.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "5 of 7 put it in their two · bar 5 of 7 · at the bar", so I know my belief held and by exactly how much, which is not at all.
screens.why_b2: The bars count 14 picks but my bar counts 7 people, and the strip's "for 5, against 9" mixes picks with people, so it takes a second look to see only 2 savers actually left inflation out.
screens.why_b3: The title Importance and the belief line are word for word what I checked, though the question's "last last 3 months" is a typo.
screens.why_b4: The So line explains that top two is not first, but it doesn't tell me what to do, e.g. that rising bills (4) run close behind inflation and my pitch should speak to both.
screens.why_b5: n is visible and "a small group: a lean, not a call" is honest, but "against 9" in a strip of 7 people reads as more against than for when only 2 were.
screens.instead: Holding up, just: 5 of 7 savers put inflation in their two, exactly at the bar, and 2 put others first. Rising bills came close (4 picks), so pitch dollars as protection for the monthly budget too, and ask more savers before leaning on it.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Holding up' sits right beside '5 of 7 said today's way falls short · bar 5 of 7 · at the bar', so I know it held and by exactly what count.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts how my 7 savers' last rupee-to-dollar conversion went, with my line drawn under 'Got dollars, paid a bit over the rate' and the strip marker at 5 of 7, all readable on first look.
screens.why_b3: 'Current solution' and 'For most savers, their way of turning leftover rupees into dollars still falls short' are word for word what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The So line breaks the gap down usefully (2 tried several places, 2 paid a big premium or took a risk, 1 got nothing), but 'judged against this gap on the next study' doesn't tell me that availability and premium are exactly what my escrowed P2P supply has to beat.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible and 'a small group: a lean, not a call' tempers a result sitting exactly at the bar, so nothing overclaims.
screens.instead: Holding up, just: 5 of 7 fell short and one fewer would miss. The gaps are finding dollars and paying a premium, which is what Karsa's verified sellers and market price must fix, so test that next.

screens.why_b1: Each box opens on 'Holding up' and repeats 'held, 5 of 7' beside 'bar 5 of 7 · at the bar', so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b3: Both belief lines are word for word the ones I checked: savings losing value to inflation in their two, and their way of turning leftover rupees into dollars still falling short.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what this means for Karsa. For example, it doesn't say that the 1-in-7 lost-to-a-seller story points at escrow trust, or that bills are the rival to address, and the 'When a line fails · 1 min' header leads nowhere.
screens.why_b5: n of 7 stays visible and nothing is called strong, but two lines that only just touch the bar with seven people are labelled 'Holding up' without saying that one more No would flip them.
screens.why_b6: The quotes add things I didn't type: monthly bills against a flat salary crowd out saving, one saver lost everything to a seller who never released and now values safe cash at home, and another tolerates forty minutes of chat a month and a few rupees over the rate.
screens.instead: Say 'Holding, exactly at the bar with 7 people: one more No flips it', and say what it means for us: the seller who never released is the trust risk escrow has to answer, and Bilal's tolerable forty-minute chat is the bar we have to beat.

screens.why1: As the first screen it makes sense to check straight away whether I earn in rupees, since the whole study is about people like me who do.
screens.why2: Rupees and income are my everyday words, so I can answer this on first reading without thinking.
screens.why3: My salary is paid in rupees and I know that without guessing.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, but someone paid partly in rupees and partly in dollars from freelance work has no clear choice, and there is no escape, which the screener rules allow.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product or a plan shows here, only a plain question about how I am paid.
screens.why6: It is short and one question, and two options are easy to hold when heard, though 'I'll read 2 options' is a bit stiff next to the guidelines' 'Yes or no.'
screens.instead: Is all or most of your income paid in rupees? Yes; or No.

screens.why1: Right after confirming I earn in rupees, asking whether I tried to get dollars with my leftover rupees in the last three months is the obvious next gate.
screens.why2: Leftover rupees into dollars is exactly how I'd say it, whether it's Binance P2P or the dealer in the market, so I can answer on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know exactly whether I tried to buy dollars these last three months and how it went.
screens.why4: Some people would answer No just because they never tried, so 'No' covers two different answers; the gate also carries two escape chips where it should have none, and 'I'd rather not say' should not exist.
screens.why5: The founder's situation is having rupees left over and wanting dollars, but 'found it hard' asks for a judgement and drops anyone who managed easily, while the next screen asks about any time I 'tried'.
screens.why6: Short, one question, and 'Yes or no' is easy to answer by ear.
screens.instead: In the last 3 months, did you try to turn rupees you had left over into dollars? Yes · No (no escape)

screens.why1: I just said yes, it was hard, so asking how often it happened in those three months is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: I understand it, but 'in the last 3 months, in how many months' makes me count twice; I think of it as each salary, not each month.
screens.why3: I change my leftover salary into dollars about once a month, so I know how many of those times were a struggle.
screens.why4: One, two or three covers it after a yes, nothing overlaps, and 'I can't recall' fits.
screens.why5: It still asks about turning leftover rupees into dollars, and nothing about a product or company reaches me.
screens.why6: It is short and 'a number from 1 to 3' is easy, but 'last 3 months, in how many months' sounds like a tongue-twister heard once.
screens.instead: Of the last 3 months, how many were hard for turning your leftover rupees into dollars? 1 · 2 · 3 · I can't recall

screens.why1: After asking how often it was hard to get dollars, asking which money worry matters most to me is a natural next step.
screens.why2: "Your last last 3 months of saving" trips me up, and "made easier" does not fit "savings losing value to inflation", because I do not want that made easier, I want it stopped.
screens.why3: These are all things I deal with every month, so I can answer from my own life.
screens.why4: My true answer is missing: getting dollars for my leftover rupees without paying the premium or chatting back and forth with a seller on Binance for every trade, and two options (inflation, rising bills) are close to the same worry.
screens.why5: Savings losing value is there, but the screen dropped what I was asked about two screens ago, turning rupees into dollars, so it has drifted away from the thing being studied.
screens.why6: Five short options is fine to hold by ear, but "your last last 3 months" sounds like a mistake when spoken, and "made easier" does not match the options as I hear them.
screens.instead: Think of the last 3 months of saving. Which one of these would you most like to be easier? Getting dollars at a fair rate; finding someone to sell dollars; not haggling in chats for each trade; keeping my dollars somewhere safe; or getting dollars back into rupees when needed. Or say none of these.

screens.why1: Asking how it went right after the hard months fits, but 'the time you described' points back to nothing: I picked months and a thing to make easier, not one particular time, and the screen before even said 'last last 3 months'.
screens.why2: Rate, premium, kept rupees: this is how we talk about the open market here, and I can answer on first reading.
screens.why3: I know exactly how my own dollar buying went these last months, what I paid over the rate and where I had to go.
screens.why4: 'Paid a big premium or took a risk' joins two different things (the open-market premium versus a risky Binance P2P chat deal), and 'tried several places' overlaps with paying over the rate, since I often did both.
screens.why5: It still means the founder's leftover rupees into dollars, and nothing of their product or their names for people reaches me.
screens.why6: Five short options are holdable, but 'paid a big premium or took a risk' puts an 'or' inside a list that ends in 'or', so by ear it sounds like two options.
screens.instead: Think of the last time you turned leftover rupees into dollars. How did it go? Got dollars near the bank rate; Paid a bit over the bank rate; Paid a big open-market premium; Bought through Binance or another app; Could not get dollars, kept rupees. Or say someone else did it.

screens.why1: I just said it went fine on the last screen, so asking what makes it go fine is the natural next thing.
screens.why2: I can answer it, but 'what keeps it working' made me stop for a second; asking how I actually do it would be plainer for me.
screens.why3: Yes, I know exactly what I do: Binance P2P with sellers I've used before, and sometimes a cousin abroad who holds the dollars for me.
screens.why4: It is a box to type in, with no options.
screens.why5: It uses my own phrase about turning leftover rupees into dollars, and nothing about any product or company comes through.
screens.why6: It is two short sentences with one question, easy to hear once and answer.
screens.instead: You said turning leftover rupees into dollars went fine. How do you usually do it?
